div.head: AGu 2
div.ab: Ðæt is ðonne, gif man ofslægen weorðe, ealle we lætað efen dyrne Engliscne ⁊ Deniscne, to VIII healfmearcum asodenes goldes, buton ðam ceorle ðe on gafollande sit ⁊ heora liesengum, ða syndan eac efen dyre: ægðer to CC scill.
⁊ hi cwædon, gyf mon ofslægen wurðe, eal we letað efen dyrne Engliscne ⁊ Denisce, þæt is to VIII healfmarcum asodenes goldes, buton ðam ceorle ðe on gafollande sit ⁊ heora lysyngon ….

Hoc autem est primum: Si quis occidatur, omnes reputamus eque carum Dacum et Anglicum, ad VIII dimidias marcas cocti auri, preter ceorlum (id est rusticum) qui in gafulland (id est in terra censaria) manet et eorum lisingun, id est redemptiones sint eque care: CC sol.

[Be ofslægenan mannes were.] Ðæt is ðonne, gif man ofslægen weorðe, ealle we lætað efen dyrne Engliscne ⁊ Deniscne, to VIII healfmearcum asodenes goldes, buton ðam ceorle ðe on gafollande sit ⁊ heora liesengum, ða syndan eac efen dyre: ægðer to CC scill.

(Vom Wergeld eines erschlagenen Mannes. Ld) Es folgt sodann (Und sie bestimmten B2): wenn ein Mensch erschlagen wird, schätzen wir einen Englischen und Dänischen ganz gleich theuer, (nämlich B2) zu 8 Halbmark geläuterten Goldes — ausser dem Gemeinfreien, der auf Zinsland sitzt, und den Freigelassenen jener [Dänen]; diese sind auch gleich theuer: jeder von beiden zu 200 Schill.

(Of the wergeld of a slain man. Ld) It follows then (And they determined B2): if a person is slain, we value an Englishman and a Dane as equally dear, (namely B2) at 8 half-marks of refined gold — except for the common freeman who sits on tributary land and the freedmen of those [Danes]; these too are equally dear: each at 200 shillings.

Secondly, if a man is slain, whether he is an Englishman or a Dane, all of us shall place the same value on his life—namely 8 half-marks of pure gold, with the exception of commoners who occupy tributary land, and freedmen of the Danes. These also shall be valued at the same amount—[namely] 200 shillings—in either case.

This is next, if a man is slain, all of us estimate Englishman and Dane at the same amount, at eight half-marks of refined gold, except the ceorl who occupies rented land, and their [the Danes’] freedmen; these also are estimated at the same amount, both at 200 shillings.

Bessere Übs.: ‘Nämlich also’. Ähnliche Anfänge ebd. 217 Sp. 3 Z. 1, auch I Em 1. IV Eg 1; þonne heisst hier ‘sodann’, im Ggs. zu ærest in 1. — Zur Form B2 (über deren 3. Person o. 1¹) vgl. I Ew 1, 2ff.; we cwædon auch u. 5. — Primum in Q ist falsch laut imprimis in 1

Better transl.: ‘Namely thus’. Similar openings ibid. 217 col. 3 l. 1, also I Em 1. IV Eg 1; þonne here means ‘then’, in contrast to ærest in 1. — On the form in B2 (on its 3rd person see above 1¹) cf. I Ew 1, 2ff.; we cwædon also below 5. — Primum in Q is wrong, given imprimis in 1

‘Voll(Über)freier’. In ähnlichem Vertrage, wo ebenfalls Engländer und Nordmann gleichstehen, setzt II Atr 5 = Hn 70, 6 ‘ein Freier einen Freien’. Gemeint ist, laut des hohen Wergelds und des Ausschlusses des Zinsbauern, der nicht nur persönlich, sondern auch im Landeigentum Freie, der echte Grundbesitzer. Hodgkin (Pol. hist. Engl. I 288¹) wundert sich, dass man steht, wo Thegn gemeint ist; vgl. aber Gl Thegn 8

‘Fully (more than) free man’. In a similar treaty, where Englishman and Northman are likewise on an equal footing, II Atr 5 = Hn 70, 6 has ‘a freeman for a freeman’. What is meant, given the high wergild and the exclusion of the tributary peasant, is the man who is free not only in person but also in the ownership of land, the true landowner. Hodgkin (Pol. hist. Engl. I 288¹) is surprised that man stands where thegn is meant; cf., however, Gl Thegn 8
S. Wb 6
See Wb 6

‘alle’ Q; ‘wir alle’ frühere Erklärer, nach Analogie von c. 5 Anfang. Mir scheint adverbialer Instrumental bzw.in B2 Accus. (Toller Suppl. 168b II 2. 3) vorzuliegen, zu efen zugehörig. Denn eine Betonung der Gesamtheit der Beschliessenden (im Ggs. zu bloss einer Partei) ist wohl in 5 am Platze, aber nicht hier. Dagegen eine Betonung der Gleichheit der Rassenschätzung entspricht dem Sinne; vgl. Gl Dänen 10

‘all’ Q; ‘we all’ earlier commentators, by analogy with the beginning of c. 5. To me it seems to be an adverbial instrumental, or in B2 an accusative (Toller Suppl. 168b II 2. 3), belonging with efen. For an emphasis on the whole body of those resolving (in contrast to only one party) is probably in place in 5, but not here. An emphasis on the equality of the valuation of the two races, on the other hand, fits the sense; cf. Gl Dänen 10
Nicht ‘7¹/₂ Mark’, wie Price wollte, da VIII nicht Ordinalzahl ist. — Vgl. Gl Gold 2. 8. 8 Halbmark (s. d. Gl 1) = 2 Pfund setzt auch Maurer Höldur 200
Not ‘7¹/₂ marks’, as Price would have it, since VIII is not an ordinal number. — Cf. Gl Gold 2. 8. Maurer Höldur 200 also equates 8 half-marks (see that word in Gl 1) with 2 pounds
Vgl. Ducange aurum coctum
Cf. Ducange aurum coctum

Nicht ‘freed-man’ (Hodgkin), sondern der persönlich Freie, und nie unfrei Gewesene, ökonomisch aber, weil ohne Grundeigen, Abhängige steht entweder infolge dieser Abhängigkeit oder aber infolge der politischen Besiegung durch Fremde nur dem unfrei Gewesenen, jetzt Freigelassenen der Sieger gleich. Nicht etwa nur Ausdrucksmangel verschuldet diese Herabdrückung des Ceorl: denn das Nordische bot für dieses Wort, das Englische für nord. leysingr etymologisch Verwandtes. Vielleicht stieg der Ostenglische Grossbauer auf echtem Eigentume zum Adel, indem sein verarmter Standesgenosse in der sozialen Stufenleiter sank; vgl. Gl Bauer 1 i. 4d. 9f

Not ‘freed-man’ (Hodgkin); rather the man who is free in person and has never been unfree, but who is economically dependent because he has no land of his own, is placed on a par merely with the conquerors' former unfree man, now a freedman, either as a result of this dependence or else as a result of political defeat by foreigners. It is not, say, merely a lack of vocabulary that is responsible for this lowering of the Ceorl: for Norse offered an etymologically related word for this one, and English for Norse leysingr. Perhaps the East Anglian large farmer on land held in full ownership rose to the nobility, while his impoverished fellow of the same rank sank on the social ladder; cf. Gl Bauer 1 i. 4d. 9f

Altnorwegisch ist leysingr der Freigelassene höherer Ordnung; Maurer Freilassung in SB Münch. Ak. 1878, 31. Noch um 1060 existierten in Ostanglien lisingas, zwar getrennt von þeowe, aber nach Urk. Ke 980 erst noch freizulassen, also Halbfreie. — Q wählt unter den zwei gleich geschriebenen Wörtern irrig das ‘Freilassung’ bedeutende Femininum

In Old Norwegian leysingr is the freedman of the higher class; Maurer Freilassung in SB Münch. Ak. 1878, 31. As late as c. 1060 there existed in East Anglia lisingas, distinct indeed from þeowe, but, according to charter Ke 980, still to be freed, and therefore half-free. — Of the two identically spelt words Q wrongly chooses the feminine, meaning ‘manumission’

Scandinavian payments are regularly reckoned by marks (A.S. marc, O. Norse mörk) and ores (A.S. ora, O. Norse eyrir, pl. aurar), which are standards of weight, 8 of the latter being equal to one of the former. In England 20 pence were commonly reckoned to the (silver) ora, though an ora of 16 pence is not unfrequently found. As the payment here is to be made in gold, the question of the relative values of gold and silver is involved (see Chadwick, Anglo-Saxon Institutions, pp. 24 f., 47 f.). The sum specified may represent a recognised Scandinavian wergeld, which is probably not very far from that of the West Saxon thegn (1200 shillings).

note.seg: Liebermann, however, takes “all” as adverbial, i.e. “precisely we estimate”.

note.label: half-marks
note.seg: A mark was a Scandinavian weight, by the end of the next century, and perhaps already, about 3440–3520 grains. The amount here stated may represent a recognised Scandinavian wergild, but, if the ratio of gold to silver was approximately 10:1 at this time, it would not be very far from the wergild of the highest English class, see Chadwick, Studies on Anglo-Saxon Institutions, pp. 50f.

note.label: land
note.seg: It is perhaps best to interpret this, as does Stenton (Anglo-Saxon England, 3rd edn, pp. 261f.), as meaning all of the ceorl class who do not farm land of their own. Those of this class who do are then classed with Englishmen of noble rank as level with all free classes of Danes. One should compare the treaty with the Danes in Ethelred’s reign (No. 42), where similarly Danish and English free men are set level and paid for at the highest wergild (£25=1200 West Saxon shillings). It would not be in itself inconceivable that the Danes might insist on lowering all English ceorlas to the level of their own half-free class, but if that were what was meant here, the relative clause would seem redundant.
